## Is it the Ghost?

It was the evening on which MM. Debienne and Poligny, the managers of the Opera, were giving a last gala performance to mark their retirement. Suddenly the dressing-room of La Sorelli, one of the principal dancers, was invaded by half-a-dozen young ladies of the ballet, who rushed in amid great confusion—some giving vent to forced and unnatural laughter, others to cries of terror. It was little Jammes—the girl with the tip-tilted nose, the forget-me-not eyes, the rose-red cheeks and the lily-white neck and shoulders—who gave the explanation in a trembling voice:

"It's the ghost!" And she locked the door.

Sorelli was very superstitious. She shuddered, called Jammes a "silly little fool," and then, being the first to believe in ghosts in general and the Opera ghost in particular, at once asked for details. The ghost had appeared to them in the shape of a gentleman in dress-clothes who had suddenly stood before them in the passage, without their knowing where he came from—seeming to have come straight through the wall.

For several months there had been nothing discussed at the Opera but this ghost in dress-clothes who stalked about the building like a shadow, spoke to nobody, vanished as soon as he was seen, and made no noise in walking. People began by laughing at this spectre dressed like a man of fashion or an undertaker; but the legend soon swelled to enormous proportions. Had any one met with a fall, suffered a practical joke, or lost a powderpuff—it was at once the fault of the ghost, of the Opera ghost.

The idea of the skeleton came from the description given by Joseph Buquet, the chief scene-shifter, who had really seen the ghost—running up against him on the little staircase by the footlights that leads to the cellars. He had seen him for only a second, for the ghost had fled; but to any one who cared to listen he said:

"He is extraordinarily thin and his dress-coat hangs on a skeleton frame. His eyes are so deep that you can hardly see the fixed pupils. You just see two big black holes, as in a dead man's skull. His skin, which is stretched across his bones like a drumhead, is not white, but a nasty yellow. His nose is so little worth talking about that you can't see it side-face; and THE ABSENCE of that nose is a horrible thing TO LOOK AT. All the hair he has is three or four long dark locks on his forehead and behind his ears."

Buquet was a serious, sober, steady man, very slow at imagining things. His words were received with interest and amazement; and soon there were other people to say that they too had met a man in dress-clothes with a death's head on his shoulders. Then a fireman who had ventured rather farther than usual in his round of the cellars suddenly reappeared on the stage, pale, scared, trembling, and practically fainted—because he had seen coming toward him, at the level of his head but without a body attached to it, a head of fire. And, as I said, a fireman is not afraid of fire. His name was Pampin; I have the anecdote from M. Pedro Gailhard himself.

Sorelli, on the day after, placed a horseshoe on the table in front of the stage-door-keeper's box, which every one who entered the Opera otherwise than as a spectator must touch before setting foot on the first tread of the staircase. This horse-shoe was not invented by me—any more than any other part of this story, alas!—and may still be seen on the table in the passage outside the stage-door-keeper's box, when you enter through the Cour de l'Administration.

To return to the evening in question.

"It's the ghost!" little Jammes had cried.

An agonizing silence now reigned in the dressing-room. Nothing was heard but the hard breathing of the girls. Then a rustling came from outside the door—not footsteps, but something like light silk sliding over the panel. Then it stopped. Sorelli armed herself with the dagger that never left her, turned the key, and drew back the door, while the ballet-girls retreated to the inner room and Meg Giry sighed: "Mother! Mother!" The passage was empty; a gas-flame cast a red and suspicious light into the surrounding darkness without dispelling it. Sorelli slammed the door again.

The talk turned to the ghost's private box—Box Five on the grand tier, next to the stage-box on the left—which Meg Giry let slip, under oath of secrecy, was reserved for the ghost alone and must never be sold. He was never seen there, but he could be heard, and her mother gave him his programme.

Little Giry was just warning that Joseph Buquet had no business to talk of things that did not concern him—it would bring him bad luck—when a breathless voice cried in the passage:

"Cecile! Are you there?"

A respectable lady built on the lines of a Pomeranian grenadier burst into the dressing-room and dropped groaning into a chair. "Joseph Buquet is dead!"

The room became filled with exclamations, with astonished outcries, with scared requests for explanation.

"He was found hanging in the third-floor cellar!"

"*It's the ghost!*" little Giry blurted, then pressed her hands to her mouth: "No, no—I didn't say it—I didn't say it—"

All around her, her panic-stricken companions repeated under their breath: "Yes—it must be the ghost!"

The truth is that no one ever knew how Joseph Buquet met his death. The verdict at the inquest was "natural suicide." In his *Memoirs of a Manager*, M. Moncharmin—one of the joint managers who succeeded Debienne and Poligny—describes how he rushed down the staircase and the Jacob's ladder, only to find that the man was no longer hanging from his rope.

So this is an event which M. Moncharmin thinks natural. A man hangs at the end of a rope; they go to cut him down; the rope has disappeared. Oh, M. Moncharmin found a very simple explanation! The corps de ballet, he suggests, had scuttled down and divided the suicide's rope among themselves as a charm against the evil eye. There you are! When, on the other hand, I think of the exact spot where the body was discovered—the third cellar underneath the stage—I imagine that SOMEBODY must have been interested in seeing that the rope disappeared after it had effected its purpose; and time will show if I am wrong.

The horrid news spread all over the Opera, where Buquet was very popular. The dressing-rooms emptied, and the ballet-girls, crowding around Sorelli like timid sheep around their shepherdess, made for the foyer through the ill-lit passages and staircases, trotting as fast as their little pink legs could carry them.
